Series::kurtosis¶

Back to SeriesStatAccessor API Reference

Signature¶

Series::stat.kurtosis() -> Series
Series::stat.kurtosis(std::int64_t dim) -> Series
Series::stat().kurtosis() -> Series
Series::stat().kurtosis(std::int64_t dim) -> Series

What It Does¶

kurtosis() measures fourth-moment shape: how heavy-tailed or sharply peaked a distribution is relative to its spread.

This implementation reports excess kurtosis, not raw Pearson kurtosis.

That distinction matters immediately:

  • a normal-like reference point is 0

  • not 3

Surface Note¶

Like skewness, the verified callable path on this surface is through the stats accessor:

  • x.stat.kurtosis(...)

  • x.stat().kurtosis(...)

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The reduced axis.

Important details:

  • omit dim to summarize the entire Series

  • pass dim to compute one kurtosis value per surviving lane

  • negative dims count from the back

Returns¶

Series A reduction result containing one excess-kurtosis value per surviving lane, or one value for the entire Series when no dim is provided.

Gradient¶

Like skewness, this is primarily a descriptive statistic used to understand distribution shape.

Verified Examples¶

The examples below are arranged to introduce the excess-kurtosis convention first, then show that asymmetry and kurtosis are different questions.

Example 1. Symmetric three-point rows produce negative excess kurtosis.

auto values = pluss::make_series(
    {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, {2, 3});

std::cout << values.stat.kurtosis(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5, -1.5]

This is the clearest “excess kurtosis” tell on the page. If you expected a normal reference around 3, you were thinking of the raw Pearson form.

Example 2. The explicit proxy spelling stat().kurtosis(dim) reaches the same row-wise computation.

std::cout << values.stat().kurtosis(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5, -1.5]

This is the same statistic as Example 1, reached through the more explicit accessor spelling.

Example 3. Lopsided rows can share the same kurtosis as symmetric rows.

auto lopsided = pluss::make_series(
    {1, 1, 4, 2, 2, 8}, {2, 3});

std::cout << lopsided.stat.kurtosis(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5, -1.5]

That is an important point:

  • kurtosis is not skewness

  • visibly lopsided lanes can still have the same excess-kurtosis summary

Example 4. Global kurtosis can differ materially from per-row kurtosis once the distribution is pooled.

std::cout << lopsided.stat.kurtosis();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.055555556]

The pooled distribution is only slightly above the normal-like zero reference here, which is very different from the row-wise -1.5 result.

Example 5. Negative dimensions count from the back, so -1 means the last axis.

std::cout << lopsided.stat.kurtosis(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.5, -1.5]

On this 2D shape, the last axis is the row axis, so the result matches Example 3.

Gotchas And Notes¶

  • This surface reports excess kurtosis.

  • Use the stats accessor path on the current public surface.

  • Kurtosis and skewness summarize different shape properties and should not be mentally collapsed into one “weirdness” metric.

  • Very short lanes can still produce a kurtosis value, but higher-moment statistics are sensitive and should be interpreted with care on small samples.

  • A dim outside the valid axis range fails.

Summary¶

Use kurtosis() when you care about tail/peakedness shape rather than center or spread:

  • excess kurtosis 0 is the normal-like reference point on this surface

  • negative values mean flatter/lighter-tailed behavior relative to that reference

  • positive values mean heavier-tailed or sharper-peaked behavior relative to that reference

  • lane-wise and global kurtosis can disagree because they summarize different pooled data

See Also¶

  • Series::skewness: asymmetry rather than tail/peakedness shape.

  • Series::standardize: transform the values instead of summarizing their fourth moment.
